title: Disjoint Set Union
why: Union-find answers 'are these two in the same group?' in near-O(1) with path compression plus union by size. It's 15 lines, and it underpins Kruskal's MST, offline connectivity, and a large class of 'merge these things' problems.
traps: Implementing only one optimisation. Path compression alone gives O(log n); with union by size/rank you get inverse-Ackermann, effectively constant.
Union by *value* instead of by root: always `find` both endpoints first, then link the roots.
DSU cannot undo a union. If the problem needs deletions, you need rollback DSU (union by rank only, no path compression) or offline processing.
Recursive `find` in Python hitting the recursion limit on a degenerate chain — write it iteratively.

template.py:
class DSU:
    __slots__ = ('p', 'sz')
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.p = list(range(n))
        self.sz = [1] * n
    def find(self, x):
        p = self.p
        while p[x] != x:                 # ITERATIVE - no recursion limit
            p[x] = p[p[x]]               # path halving
            x = p[x]
        return x
    def unite(self, a, b):
        a, b = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if a == b: return False
        if self.sz[a] < self.sz[b]: a, b = b, a
        self.p[b] = a
        self.sz[a] += self.sz[b]
        return True

pyNote: Path *halving* (`p[x] = p[p[x]]` inside a while loop) gives the same amortised bound as recursive full compression while staying iterative — this is the right Python implementation.
checkpoint: You can write DSU from memory in under two minutes and use it to count connected components after each of q edge additions.

title: Tree Fundamentals
why: A tree is a connected acyclic graph with n-1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices. Rooting it turns the structure into parent/child relations, and one DFS gives you depth, subtree size, and Euler tour times — the inputs to almost every tree algorithm above this point.
traps: Not skipping the parent when recursing, causing infinite back-and-forth on undirected edges.
Assuming vertex 1 is the root. Some problems specify a root; others let you choose (pick 1, but say so).
Recursion depth again: a path graph of 10^5 nodes is a legal tree. Iterative DFS in Python, always.
Confusing depth (edges from root) with height (edges to the deepest descendant).

template.py:
par = [0]*(n+1); dep = [0]*(n+1); sz = [1]*(n+1)

# iterative: build an order, then process it in reverse for subtree sums
order, stack = [], [1]
par[1] = 0
seen = [False]*(n+1); seen[1] = True
while stack:
    u = stack.pop()
    order.append(u)
    for v in adj[u]:
        if not seen[v]:
            seen[v] = True
            par[v] = u
            dep[v] = dep[u] + 1
            stack.append(v)

for u in reversed(order):                   # reverse BFS/DFS order = post-order
    if par[u]: sz[par[u]] += sz[u]

pyNote: The `reversed(order)` idiom is the cleanest iterative post-order in Python: collect vertices in DFS/BFS order, then walk backwards. Every child is processed before its parent, which is exactly what subtree aggregation needs.
checkpoint: You can compute subtree sizes and answer 'is u an ancestor of v' in O(1) after one DFS.

title: DP on Trees
why: Compute an answer for each subtree from its children's answers. The state is usually dp[u][something-small]; the transition combines children. Rerooting extends this to 'the answer for every possible root' in O(n) total rather than O(n^2).
traps: Combining children in a way that double-counts a path through u. For path problems, combine children pairwise but count each pair once.
Leaf base cases forgotten, so leaves inherit garbage.
Recursion depth (Python) — use the reverse-order iterative pattern.
Rerooting without correctly 'removing' the current subtree's contribution from the parent's aggregate — especially painful when the combiner isn't invertible (use prefix/suffix aggregates instead).

template.py:
# iterative tree DP using the reverse-order trick
dp0 = [0]*(n+1)
dp1 = val[:]                       # dp1[u] starts as val[u]

for u in reversed(order):          # children before parents
    p = par[u]
    if p:
        dp0[p] += max(dp0[u], dp1[u])
        dp1[p] += dp0[u]

answer = max(dp0[root], dp1[root])

pyNote: Iterative tree DP in Python is genuinely pleasant with the reverse-order pattern: no recursion, and you push each child's finished value into its parent as you go.
checkpoint: You can compute the tree diameter and solve maximum-independent-set-on-a-tree iteratively.

title: Topological Sort & DAG DP
why: Order a DAG so every edge points forward. That order is exactly the valid evaluation order for DP on a DAG — longest path, path counting, reachability — all of which are trivial once sorted and NP-hard on general graphs.
traps: Not detecting cycles. If Kahn's algorithm outputs fewer than n vertices, a cycle exists — check this, many problems hinge on it.
Assuming the topological order is unique. It usually isn't; if the problem wants lexicographically smallest, use a priority queue instead of a plain queue.
Longest path on a DAG is easy, but on a graph with cycles it's NP-hard. Verify acyclicity first.
Forgetting that a DAG can be disconnected — seed the queue with every zero-indegree vertex.
checkpoint: You can detect a cycle and compute the longest path on a DAG in one pass.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
why: Single-source shortest paths with **non-negative** weights in O((V+E) log V). The workhorse of shortest-path problems, and the base for layered-graph tricks where you add extra state to the node (e.g. 'shortest path using at most k free edges').
traps: **Negative weights break it.** Dijkstra can finalise a node too early. Use Bellman-Ford or SPFA if any weight is negative.
Not using lazy deletion: pop a (d, u) pair and skip it if d > dist[u], otherwise you process stale entries.
`int` overflow on distances — sum of 2*10^5 edges of weight 10^9 is 2*10^14. Use `long long` / a large INF like 4e18 that won't overflow when added to.
Initialising INF to `INT_MAX` then computing `INF + w`, which overflows. Use a sentinel with headroom.

template.py:
import heapq
INF = float('inf')

dist = [INF] * (n + 1)
dist[src] = 0
pq = [(0, src)]

while pq:
    d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
    if d > dist[u]: continue               # stale
    for v, w in wadj[u]:
        nd = d + w
        if nd < dist[v]:
            dist[v] = nd
            heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))

pyNote: `float('inf')` compares correctly against ints and never overflows, so Python sidesteps the INF-overflow trap entirely. Dijkstra in CPython on a 2*10^5-edge graph is tight — submit as PyPy.
checkpoint: You can solve a layered-graph Dijkstra (extra state per node) without rewriting the core loop.

title: 0-1 BFS & Deque Tricks
why: When every edge weight is 0 or 1, a deque replaces the heap: push weight-0 edges to the front and weight-1 edges to the back. You get O(V+E) instead of O(E log V), and the idea generalises to small integer weights via dial's algorithm.
traps: Pushing to the wrong end. Zero-weight to the **front**, one-weight to the back — reversed, the distances are simply wrong.
Forgetting the staleness check. Nodes can enter the deque multiple times; skip if the popped distance is worse than the recorded one.
Applying it to weights other than 0 and 1.
Not recognising the pattern: 'minimum number of changes/flips/blocks removed' is very often 0-1 BFS in disguise.
checkpoint: You can recognise a 'minimum obstacles removed' grid problem as 0-1 BFS and solve it without a heap.

title: DP on Grids & Paths
why: The gentlest 2D DP: dp[i][j] depends on dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. It builds the habit of thinking about iteration order and rolling-array space optimisation, both of which transfer to every harder DP.
traps: Wrong iteration order, using a cell before it's computed.
Blocked cells not excluded from transitions — they must contribute nothing, not zero-as-a-valid-value.
Memory: a 5000x5000 `long long` table is 200 MB. Roll to two rows, or one row if the transition allows.
Counting paths without a modulus when the count exceeds 64 bits.

template.py:
dp = [[0]*m for _ in range(n)]
dp[0][0] = 1 if g[0][0] == '.' else 0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(m):
        if g[i][j] == '#':
            dp[i][j] = 0
            continue
        if i: dp[i][j] += dp[i-1][j]
        if j: dp[i][j] += dp[i][j-1]
        dp[i][j] %= MOD

# rolling array
prev = [0]*m
for i in range(n):
    cur = [0]*m
    ...
    prev = cur

checkpoint: You can convert any 2D grid DP to O(m) memory with a rolling array.

title: LIS & Sequence DP
why: Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n) via the patience-sorting tail array — and more importantly, the realisation that many sequence problems reduce to LIS after a transformation (reverse one array, negate, map to positions).
traps: Strictly vs non-strictly increasing changes `lower_bound` to `upper_bound`. This one character is the whole difference.
The tail array is **not** the actual LIS — its length is correct but its contents generally aren't a valid subsequence. Reconstruct with parent pointers if you need the sequence itself.
Applying the O(n log n) version to a problem needing LIS *counts* — that requires a Fenwick tree instead.
Not recognising a disguised LIS: 'maximum matching pairs between two permutations' is usually LIS after remapping.

template.py:
import bisect

tails = []
for x in a:
    i = bisect.bisect_left(tails, x)      # bisect_right for non-strict
    if i == len(tails): tails.append(x)
    else: tails[i] = x
lis = len(tails)

pyNote: `bisect_left` vs `bisect_right` maps exactly onto strict vs non-strict LIS, and the whole algorithm is six lines — this is one of the cases where the Python version is clearly cleaner than C++.
checkpoint: You can write LIS in O(n log n), handle both strictness variants, and reconstruct the actual subsequence.

title: Bitmask DP
why: When n <= 20, the subset itself can be the DP state. dp[mask] over 2^n subsets solves travelling salesman, assignment problems, and 'partition into groups' — all NP-hard in general but perfectly tractable at this size.
traps: Misjudging the complexity: TSP is O(2^n * n^2), which at n = 20 is ~4*10^8 — too slow in Python, borderline in C++. Check before committing.
Iterating masks out of order. Process in increasing mask order so subsets are computed before supersets.
Memory: dp[1<<20][20] of `long long` is 168 MB. Use `int` where possible, or restructure.
Submask enumeration is O(3^n) total, not O(4^n) — but only if you use the `(sub-1) & mask` idiom.

template.py:
INF = float('inf')
dp = [[INF]*n for _ in range(1 << n)]
dp[1][0] = 0
for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
    row = dp[mask]
    for i in range(n):
        if not (mask >> i & 1) or row[i] == INF: continue
        for j in range(n):
            if mask >> j & 1: continue
            nm = mask | (1 << j)
            nd = row[i] + cost[i][j]
            if nd < dp[nm][j]: dp[nm][j] = nd

pyNote: Bitmask DP is the clearest case where Python struggles: 2^20 * 20 * 20 Python-level operations will TLE even on PyPy. For n >= 18, write these in C++.
checkpoint: You can solve TSP for n = 15 and explain why submask enumeration totals 3^n.

title: Digit DP
why: Count numbers in [L, R] satisfying a digit-wise property, where R can be 10^18. You build the number digit by digit, carrying a 'tight' flag that says whether you're still hugging the upper bound. The count for [L, R] is f(R) - f(L-1).
traps: Forgetting the leading-zero state. '007' and '7' differ for properties like 'number of distinct digits'.
Memoising across different tight values. Only cache states where tight is false — tight states are visited once each anyway.
Off-by-one on the range: f(R) - f(L-1), not f(R) - f(L).
Not resetting the memo table between test cases when the bound changes.
pyNote: `@lru_cache` handles the tight flag correctly as part of the key, so the Python version needs no manual 'only cache when not tight' logic — just remember `cache_clear()` between bounds. Digit DP has few states, so recursion depth (~19) is never a problem here.
checkpoint: You can count numbers up to 10^18 with a given digit-sum property in under 40 lines.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree
why: Kruskal is 'sort edges, add if they connect two different components' — DSU plus five lines. Beyond the plain MST, the same sorted-edge sweep answers 'minimum bottleneck path' and powers offline connectivity problems.
traps: Forgetting to check that the MST actually spans: if you added fewer than n-1 edges, the graph is disconnected.
Sorting by weight but comparing whole edge tuples, so equal weights break ties by endpoint in a way the problem didn't intend.
Using Prim with an adjacency matrix on a sparse graph — that's O(n^2) when Kruskal would be O(E log E).
Maximum spanning tree is the same algorithm with the sort reversed; don't rewrite it.
checkpoint: You can build an MST with Kruskal and detect disconnected input.

title: Floyd-Warshall
why: All-pairs shortest paths in O(n^3), in three nested loops. For n <= 400 it's simply the easiest correct answer, it tolerates negative edges, and the same loop structure computes transitive closure and minimum-bottleneck paths.
traps: **The k loop must be outermost.** Any other order is silently wrong. This is the single most common Floyd-Warshall bug.
Overflow from INF + INF. Guard with `if (d[i][k] == INF || d[k][j] == INF) continue;` or use a padded INF.
Not initialising `d[i][i] = 0`, and not handling multi-edges (keep the minimum).
Using it at n = 2000, which is 8*10^9 operations.

template.py:
INF = float('inf')
d = [[INF]*n for _ in range(n)]
for i in range(n): d[i][i] = 0
for u, v, w in edges: d[u][v] = min(d[u][v], w)

for k in range(n):                             # k OUTERMOST
    dk = d[k]
    for i in range(n):
        di = d[i]
        dik = di[k]
        if dik == INF: continue
        for j in range(n):
            nd = dik + dk[j]
            if nd < di[j]: di[j] = nd

pyNote: Hoisting `d[i]` and `d[k]` into locals before the inner loop is the standard Python optimisation here — it removes two list index operations per iteration and can nearly halve the runtime. Still, n^3 in Python means n <= ~150 on CPython, ~400 on PyPy.
checkpoint: You can write Floyd-Warshall with k outermost from memory and detect negative cycles.

title: Bellman-Ford & Negative Cycles
why: The shortest-path algorithm that tolerates negative weights, in O(V*E). Its real value in contests is *detecting* negative cycles — if a distance still improves on the n-th round, a negative cycle is reachable.
traps: Running n-1 rounds and concluding there's no negative cycle. You need an n-th round to detect one.
Reporting a negative cycle that isn't reachable from the source, when the problem only cares about reachable ones.
Not tracking predecessors when the problem asks you to output the cycle itself.
Using it when Dijkstra would do — O(V*E) is 2*10^10 at V=E=10^5.

template.py:
INF = float('inf')
dist = [INF]*n
dist[src] = 0
par = [-1]*n
last = -1
for _ in range(n):
    last = -1
    for u, v, w in edges:
        if dist[u] < INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            dist[v] = dist[u] + w
            par[v] = u
            last = v

has_negative_cycle = last != -1

checkpoint: You can detect a negative cycle and reconstruct the vertices on it.

title: Sparse Table
why: O(1) range minimum/maximum/gcd queries after O(n log n) preprocessing. It only works for **idempotent** operations and a **static** array — but when those hold, nothing beats it for simplicity and speed.
traps: Using it for range *sum*. Sums aren't idempotent, so the overlapping-blocks trick double-counts. Use prefix sums or a Fenwick tree.
No updates allowed. Any modification means rebuilding the whole table.
Off-by-one in the level calculation: for range [l, r] the level is `log2(r - l + 1)`, and the two blocks are `[l, l+2^k-1]` and `[r-2^k+1, r]`.
Memory: n log n entries. At n = 10^6 that's 2*10^7 ints — 80 MB. Watch the limit.

template.py:
LOG = n.bit_length()
sp = [a[:]]
k = 1
while (1 << k) <= n:
    prev = sp[-1]
    half = 1 << (k - 1)
    sp.append([min(prev[i], prev[i + half]) for i in range(n - (1 << k) + 1)])
    k += 1

def query(l, r):                            # inclusive
    k = (r - l + 1).bit_length() - 1
    return min(sp[k][l], sp[k][r - (1 << k) + 1])

pyNote: Building each level with a list comprehension keeps the work in C. `int.bit_length()` replaces `__lg` exactly and is a built-in.
checkpoint: You can answer 10^6 range-minimum queries in O(1) each, and explain why sums don't work.

title: Binary Lifting & LCA
why: Precompute the 2^k-th ancestor of every node, then jump to any ancestor in O(log n). That gives lowest common ancestor, distance between any two nodes, and 'the k-th node on a path' — the foundation of most tree query problems.
traps: Not handling the case where one node is an ancestor of the other; lift the deeper node first, then check for equality before the second phase.
Sizing LOG too small. You need `LOG > log2(n)`; at n = 2*10^5 that's 18, so use 20.
Using a 0 sentinel for 'no ancestor' while also having a real node 0. Pick one convention.
Building the table with a recursive DFS in Python and blowing the stack.
pyNote: Index the table as `up[k][v]`, not `up[v][k]` — it lets you hoist the whole level list into a local and keeps the build loop cache- and interpreter-friendly.
checkpoint: You can answer 10^5 LCA and path-distance queries on a 10^5-node tree.

title: Extended Euclid, Euler & CRT
why: Extended Euclid gives modular inverses for *any* coprime modulus, not just primes. Euler's totient counts coprimes and generalises Fermat. Together they solve linear congruences and the Chinese Remainder Theorem — staples of ICPC math problems.
traps: Assuming the modulus is prime and reaching for Fermat when it isn't. Extended Euclid is the general tool.
ax ≡ b (mod m) has a solution only when gcd(a, m) divides b — check before dividing.
Overflow in CRT: combining two moduli near 10^9 gives a product near 10^18, and intermediate multiplications overflow. Use __int128 in C++.
Computing phi(n) by trial division per query when a sieve would give all values up to n at once.

template.py:
from math import gcd

def egcd(a, b):
    if b == 0: return a, 1, 0
    g, x1, y1 = egcd(b, a % b)
    return g, y1, x1 - (a // b) * y1

# built-in, no modulus-is-prime requirement:
inv = pow(a, -1, m)                        # raises ValueError if not coprime

# totient sieve
phi = list(range(N))
for i in range(2, N):
    if phi[i] == i:
        for j in range(i, N, i):
            phi[j] -= phi[j] // i

# CRT - no overflow ever, thanks to big ints
def crt(r1, m1, r2, m2):
    g, p, q = egcd(m1, m2)
    if (r2 - r1) % g: return None
    lcm = m1 // g * m2
    x = (r1 + (r2 - r1) // g * p % (m2 // g) * m1) % lcm
    return x % lcm, lcm

pyNote: CRT is a place where Python's arbitrary-precision ints are a genuine advantage — the C++ version needs `__int128` to avoid overflow when combining moduli, while Python just works.
checkpoint: You can solve ax ≡ b (mod m) for non-prime m and combine two congruences with CRT.

title: Meet in the Middle
why: Turns 2^n into 2^(n/2). Split the input in half, enumerate all subsets of each half, then combine with sorting plus binary search. At n = 40 this converts an impossible 10^12 into a very comfortable 10^6.
traps: Forgetting the combine step is itself O(2^(n/2) log(2^(n/2))) — sort one half once, don't re-sort per query.
Splitting unevenly. Halves should differ by at most one element.
Not deduplicating or not using prefix maxima when the combine needs 'best value with sum <= x'.
Memory: 2^20 entries per half is 10^6 — fine — but 2^25 is not.

template.py:
from itertools import combinations
import bisect

h1 = n // 2
left, right = a[:h1], a[h1:]

def all_sums(arr):
    res = []
    for m in range(1 << len(arr)):
        res.append(sum(arr[i] for i in range(len(arr)) if m >> i & 1))
    return res

A, B = all_sums(left), sorted(all_sums(right))

best = 0
for x in A:
    i = bisect.bisect_right(B, K - x)
    if i: best = max(best, x + B[i-1])

checkpoint: You can solve subset-sum for n = 40 within the time limit.

title: Interactive Problems
why: You query a judge and adapt. Nearly all of them are binary search, ternary search, or an adaptive guessing strategy under a strict query budget. The mechanics — flushing after every query — are trivial but unforgiving.
traps: **Not flushing.** Your query sits in the buffer, the judge waits, you get an idleness-limit verdict. Flush after every single output.
Exceeding the query budget by one. Compute the worst case: binary search on [1, 10^9] needs 30 queries, so a limit of 30 is exactly tight and an off-by-one kills you.
Not reading the judge's response before sending the next query.

Assuming the judge is static. Many are adaptive and will choose the answer that makes your strategy worst-case — so your solution must be correct against an adversary, not just against a fixed hidden value.

template.py:
import sys

def ask(x):
    print('?', x, flush=True)          # flush=True is MANDATORY
    r = int(input())
    if r == -1: sys.exit(0)
    return r

lo, hi = 1, 10**9
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if ask(mid) >= 0: hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1

print('!', lo, flush=True)

pyNote: Do **not** use the `input = sys.stdin.readline` speed-up trick in interactive problems without care, and always pass `flush=True` to `print`. Buffered output is the number-one cause of failed interactive submissions in Python.
checkpoint: You can solve a 30-query binary-search interactive problem with no idleness-limit verdicts.

title: ICPC: Team Strategy
why: ICPC is three people, one computer, five hours, and a penalty for every wrong submission. The team that reads all problems early and schedules the machine well beats the team with the strongest individual coder. This is a skill you practise, not one you improvise on contest day.
traps: All three reading problems in the same order. Split the problem set immediately — one takes the front, one the back, one the middle.
Debugging at the keyboard. If a submission fails, move off the machine, debug on paper, and let a teammate code the next problem.
Not tracking which problems are solved by how many teams. The scoreboard is your difficulty oracle — always work on the problem most other teams have solved.
Ignoring the penalty. A wrong submission costs 20 minutes; test against the samples and think once more before submitting.
No plan for the last hour: decide in advance when to stop starting new problems and start finishing partial ones.

template.cpp:
/*  A workable five-hour shape:

    0:00-0:15   All three read. Split A-D / E-H / I-L. Rank by
                "looks easy" and by scoreboard once it opens.
    0:15-1:30   Strongest implementer takes the easiest problems and
                clears them fast. Others think on paper.
    1:30-4:00   Rotate the machine. Rule: you only sit down when your
                solution is fully designed. Thinking happens on paper.
    4:00-4:45   Finish what is close. Stop starting new problems.
    4:45-5:00   Last submissions. Do not risk a penalty on a guess.

    Standing rules:
    - Code on paper first for anything non-trivial.
    - A second person reads the statement before any submission.
    - Failed submission => leave the keyboard, debug on paper.
    - Keep a printed team notebook; do not re-derive templates.      */
template.py:
#  Language split is a real team asset:
#  - Python for big-integer math, string manipulation, quick brute
#    forces, and generating test data while a teammate codes.
#  - C++ for anything with tight time limits or heavy data structures.
#
#  Decide the language per problem in the first 60 seconds, not after
#  a TLE. If n is large and the loop is hot, it is a C++ problem.

pyNote: In a team contest, Python's value is disproportionately in the *support* role: writing the brute force to stress-test a teammate's C++ solution, and handling the one problem with 10^1000-digit arithmetic.
checkpoint: You have run at least one five-hour practice contest as a team with an explicit machine-rotation plan.

title: ICPC: The Team Notebook
why: ICPC allows a printed reference. A good notebook means you never re-derive a segment tree under time pressure — you type it from a page you've already tested. Building it is also the best possible revision: you cannot write a clean template for something you don't understand.
traps: Copying templates you've never run. Every entry must have been used to solve at least one real problem.
Making it too long. 25 dense pages you know beats 60 you have to search. Include a table of contents.
Templates with external dependencies or non-obvious calling conventions. Each entry needs a one-line usage comment.
Leaving it until the week before. Build it incrementally as you learn each topic — that's the point.
Not testing the printed version. Typing from paper reveals ambiguous formatting, wrapped lines, and lost indentation.

template.cpp:
/*  Suggested contents, roughly in priority order:

    Graphs        DSU, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, MST,
                  topological sort, SCC, bridges/articulation, 2-SAT,
                  max flow (Dinic), min-cost max-flow, bipartite matching
    Trees         LCA (binary lifting), HLD, centroid decomposition,
                  Euler tour + BIT
    Structures    Fenwick (1D/2D), segment tree, lazy segment tree,
                  sparse table, DSU with rollback, Mo's algorithm
    Strings       KMP, Z-function, hashing (double mod), trie,
                  suffix array + LCP, Aho-Corasick
    Math          sieve, extended Euclid, CRT, nCr mod p, Miller-Rabin,
                  Pollard's rho, matrix power, FFT/NTT
    Geometry      point struct, cross/dot, segment intersection,
                  convex hull, polygon area, closest pair
    Misc          fast I/O, random, bitset tricks, ternary search

    Format rule: every entry gets a one-line description, the
    complexity, and a usage example. Nothing else.                  */
template.py:
#  Keep a parallel Python section for the handful of things Python
#  does better under time pressure:
#
#    - big-integer arithmetic (factorials, 10^1000 inputs)
#    - fractions.Fraction for exact rational geometry
#    - itertools brute forces for stress testing
#    - decimal.Decimal with high precision
#    - the big-int-as-bitset subset-sum trick
#
#  Everything else should be C++ in a team contest.

checkpoint: You have a printed, table-of-contents'd notebook where every template has solved a real problem.
